edits.walkthrough_append: **EXAM TRAP:** The vertex of y² = 4ax sits at the ORIGIN with the x-axis as its axis — shifting the vertex to (h, k) gives (y − k)² = 4a(x − h); forgetting the shift substitution, or writing y = 4ax² with the parameter misplaced, loses the equation mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** Rays parallel to the axis reflect THROUGH THE FOCUS, and rays leaving the focus emerge parallel to the axis — reversing the two directions, or applying the property to rays through the vertex (which reflect at an angle), is the standard application slip in satellite-dish and headlight questions.

**EXAM TRAP:** The derivative dy/dx is a RATE (units of y per unit of x), not the ratio of two separate numbers — and differentiability requires continuity, but continuity does NOT guarantee differentiability (|x| at 0 is the standard counterexample); stating the converse as true loses the conceptual mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** The first-principles limit requires the increment h → 0 from BOTH sides — evaluating the right-hand limit only, or substituting h = 0 before simplifying (giving 0/0), breaks the derivation; the derivative exists only when both one-sided difference quotients agree.

**EXAM TRAP:** d/dx(xⁿ) = n·xⁿ⁻¹ works for ALL real n — including negative and fractional powers (x^(1/2) → 1/(2√x)) — and the derivative of a CONSTANT is 0; treating √x or 1/x as non-differentiable by formula, or forgetting the constant rule, costs easy marks.

**EXAM TRAP:** The chain rule multiplies OUTER-derivative × INNER-derivative — d/dx f(g(x)) = f′(g(x))·g′(x) — and forgetting to multiply by the inner derivative is the single most common calculus error; working outward-in in one pass (no skipped factors) protects the mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** Two data sets can share the SAME mean with wildly different spreads — dispersion measures exist precisely because averages conceal variability; and the standard deviation is the square root of the VARIANCE — quoting variance when SD is asked (or forgetting to square in the first place) is the standard slip.

**EXAM TRAP:** Positive skewness means MEAN > MEDIAN > MODE (long right tail) — reversing the order for negative skew, or reading the tail direction from the peak instead of the elongated side, is the standard interpretation error; kurtosis measures TAIL WEIGHT, not peak height alone.

**EXAM TRAP:** Pearson's coefficient uses (Mean − Mode)/σ or 3(Mean − Median)/σ — both must be divided by the standard deviation; leaving the numerator undivided, or applying the median version when the mode is available and inconsistent, loses the computation mark; sign carries the skew direction.

**EXAM TRAP:** Kurtosis compares TAIL weight to the normal curve — leptokurtic (kurtosis > 3) has heavy tails, platykurtic (< 3) light tails — describing kurtosis as "peakedness alone" is imprecise; and both coefficients are DIMENSIONLESS, so quoting units on them is itself an error.

**EXAM TRAP:** Probable error = 0.6745 × (1 − r²)/√n — it tests whether r is SIGNIFICANT, not the probability of an error occurring; and R² is the square of r, always between 0 and 1 even when r is negative — reading a negative R² off a calculation flags an arithmetic slip.

**EXAM TRAP:** R² = 0.64 means 64% of the variation in y is explained by x LINEARLY — the remaining 36% is NOT explained, not "error in measurement" — and R² near 1 does not prove causation; writing "R² of 0.64 means r = 0.64" squares-or-roots in the wrong direction and loses the interpretation mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** b_yx × b_xy = r², so the product is always positive and cannot exceed 1 — a product greater than 1 signals an arithmetic error — and both regression coefficients share the sign of r; quoting a negative product or forgetting the r² link loses the consistency check mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** b_yx is the slope of y ON x (change in y per unit x) — swapping the subscripts answers a different question; and b_yx = r·(σ_y/σ_x), so the sign of every regression coefficient matches the sign of r — one wrong sigma ratio flips the whole line.

**EXAM TRAP:** tan θ = |(b_yx − b_xy)/(1 + b_yx·b_xy)| — the PLUS sign in the denominator is standard, and θ is the ACUTE angle between the lines; when b_yx·b_xy = 1 the lines are PERPENDICULAR (r = ±1) — using the minus sign or reporting the obtuse angle loses the mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** P(not A) = 1 − P(A) — the complement rule is the fastest route for "at least one" questions; and probabilities of individual outcomes need EQUALLY LIKELY outcomes — summing favourable-to-total ratios for biased dice as if fair is the standard misapplication.

**EXAM TRAP:** Classical probability requires EQUALLY LIKELY and EXHAUSTIVE outcomes — it cannot assign P(head) on a biased coin; and for mutually exclusive events P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) but the + rule fails when events overlap without subtracting P(A∩B) — the classic two-mark trap.

**EXAM TRAP:** EAR = (1 + r/n)ⁿ − 1 grows with n — comparing a quarterly compounding offer against an annual one using NOMINAL rates picks the wrong account; the EAR is the comparison currency, and continuous compounding gives the ceiling value e^r − 1.

**EXAM TRAP:** A = Pe^{rt} is the LIMIT of compounding as frequency → infinity, so it ALWAYS exceeds discrete compounding at the same nominal rate — treating e^{rt} as an approximation to understate growth, or mixing t in years with r per period, loses the limit-logic mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** e^r − 1 is the effective annual rate under continuous compounding — for r = 10% that is about 10.52%, NOT 10%; using e^{rt} with r as a percent number instead of a decimal (0.10) is the computational slip the numerical answers expose instantly.

**EXAM TRAP:** Future value compounds FORWARD: FV = PV(1 + i)ⁿ — every year count and rate must match the COMPOUNDING period; and an annuity's FV assumes payments at period END (ordinary) unless the question says otherwise, where the extra (1 + i) factor for annuity-due is the difference.

**EXAM TRAP:** The three pillars — compound amount, annuity, present value — answer different questions: growth of a lump sum, growth of instalments, and what a future stream is worth TODAY; using the FV formula where PV is asked (or vice versa) is the standard exam mix-up that the unit of the answer exposes.

**EXAM TRAP:** An annuity DUE pays at the START of each period, so its present value is the ordinary annuity's PV × (1 + i) — always LARGER; comparing due versus ordinary values without the (1 + i) factor, or reversing which is larger, loses the distinction mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** Residential status turns on PHYSICAL PRESENCE counts in the previous year — the 182-day basic rule plus the 60-days/365-days extended rule for certain persons — and citizenship is irrelevant to it; applying the 60-day rule to every individual, or counting stay across multiple previous years incorrectly, loses the status mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** GTI is the sum of incomes under FIVE heads — salary, house property, business/profession, capital gains, other sources — and each receipt enters exactly ONE head; excluding exempt incomes (like agricultural income) from GTI, or double-counting a receipt under two heads, are the two classification errors the question tests.

**EXAM TRAP:** A binary operation must be CLOSED — combining two set elements must yield another element OF THE SET (division on natural numbers fails because 3 ÷ 2 ∉ N); checking closure FIRST, then commutativity and associativity, is the marking order; a + b = a always is commutative but has no identity.

**EXAM TRAP:** Differentiation and integration are INVERSE processes — d/dx of ∫f(x)dx returns f(x), but the constant of integration C never disappears in indefinite integrals; forgetting C, or treating a definite integral as a function, are the two standard boundary errors.

**EXAM TRAP:** The exponential distribution is MEMORYLESS — P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t) — a property unique to it among continuous distributions; and its mean is 1/λ, the RECIPROCAL of the Poisson rate, not λ itself; swapping the two loses the parameterisation mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** The simplex method moves along EDGES of the feasible region improving the objective at each pivot — it never leaves feasibility; a negative entry in the objective row signals improvement is still possible, while all-non-negative rows mark optimality — misreading the stopping condition loops the tableau endlessly.

**EXAM TRAP:** Inverse trig answers must stay inside PRINCIPAL-VALUE ranges — sin⁻¹ returns [−π/2, π/2], cos⁻¹ returns [0, π], tan⁻¹ returns (−π/2, π/2) — writing sin⁻¹(sin 5π/3) as 5π/3 instead of reducing to the principal branch is the classic slip; and sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2 for all x ∈ [−1, 1].

**EXAM TRAP:** Rank = number of non-zero rows in Echelon form, and the system AX = B is consistent only when rank(A) = rank([A|B]) — uniqueness further needs rank = n (unknowns); declaring "no solution" from a zero row without comparing ranks loses the classification mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** Optimisation answers live at MARGINAL equality — MR = MC — not at revenue maximisation alone; and the profit function must also satisfy the SECOND-order condition (second derivative negative) for a maximum, since a stationary point can be a minimum — skipping the check loses the verification mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** π(x) = R(x) − C(x) is maximised where MR = MC AND d²π/dx² < 0 — reporting the critical point without confirming concavity can present a loss-minimising output as "optimal"; also, fixed costs do not affect the optimal OUTPUT, only whether production is profitable at all.

**EXAM TRAP:** An LPP optimum occurs at a VERTEX (corner point) of the feasible region — checking only the intersection of two constraint lines without testing ALL corner points (including axis intercepts) can report a non-optimal vertex; and an unbounded feasible region may make the objective unbounded, which is an answer, not an error.

**EXAM TRAP:** The simplex pivot column holds the most NEGATIVE entry in the objective row, and the pivot row is chosen by the MINIMUM non-negative ratio test — skipping the ratio test allows infeasible pivots; when no negative entry remains, the current vertex IS optimal, and further pivoting worsens the objective.

**EXAM TRAP:** The EMI formula needs the MONTHLY rate (annual ÷ 12) with n in months — mixing annual rate with monthly n overstates the EMI several-fold; and every EMI splits between interest (on the outstanding balance) and principal, so the interest portion FALLS over the tenure, never stays constant.

**EXAM TRAP:** Every transaction is an event, but events like appointing a manager or receiving a quotation are NOT transactions — measurability in money, dual aspect, and voucher evidence must all hold; classifying a non-monetary happening as a transaction because it "affects business" is the standard mark-loser.

**EXAM TRAP:** An internal event like charging depreciation IS a transaction (no outsider needed) as long as it is measurable, dual-aspect, and vouched — and a credit purchase creates TWO effects (goods in, creditor out); requiring an outsider for every transaction misses internal adjustments and loses the classification mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** Capital = Assets − Liabilities is the RESIDUAL claim — it increases with profits and fresh investment, and DECREASES with drawings and losses; treating drawings as an expense (debiting P&L) instead of debiting capital is the classic error, and "owner's loan to the business" is a liability, not capital.

**EXAM TRAP:** Fixed assets are held for USE, not resale — stock destined for sale is a CURRENT asset however durable it looks; and depreciation applies to fixed assets except land (which does not wear out), a pair of distinctions that classification questions always target.

**EXAM TRAP:** Liabilities are obligations to OUTSIDERS — the owner's capital claim is not a liability; and current versus non-current turns on the 12-month settlement window, so a loan due in 14 months is long-term even if the ledger shows it this year — the classification test, not the ledger date, decides.

**EXAM TRAP:** Debtors arise from CREDIT sales, not cash sales — a cash customer never becomes a debtor; and the provision for doubtful debts reduces the debtors' realisable value but debtors themselves stay at gross amount — writing "debtors are shown net of provision in the ledger" confuses final-accounts presentation with ledger records.

**EXAM TRAP:** Loss decreases capital exactly as profit increases it — and a loss is different from an EXPENSE: expenses arise in ordinary operations, loss from non-ordinary events (theft, fire without insurance); debiting a fire loss to Trading A/c instead of P&L misclassifies it and loses the placement mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** Each transaction hits at least TWO accounts with EQUAL debits and credits — the dual aspect never bends; and identifying the correct ACCOUNT CLASS (personal, real, nominal) before applying debit-credit rules is where marks are decided — applying nominal rules to a personal account (or vice versa) loses every entry mark downstream.

**EXAM TRAP:** Input CGST set-off applies against output CGST FIRST, then against IGST — never output SGST; the cross-utilisation order is exactly what the question tests, and writing input CGST against SGST liability reverses the statutory scheme and loses the set-off mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** An analytical petty cash book records payments under ANALYSIS COLUMNS (conveyance, postage, stationery) so period-end totals post straight to each expense head — the receipt side holds only the imprest reimbursement; writing each small payment individually into the main cash book defeats the columnar purpose and loses the design mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** Under the IMPREST system the petty cashier is reimbursed EXACTLY what was spent, restoring the float to its fixed maximum — reimbursing the full float regardless of spend, or treating the float itself as an expense, misreads the system; and the main-cash-book entry appears only at reimbursement.

**EXAM TRAP:** Favourable balances start the BRS from OPPOSITE sides — cash book debit (asset) matches pass book credit; and cheques issued but NOT yet presented are added back when starting from the cash book balance — mixing the adjustment directions (or treating a bank charge as increasing the balance) loses the reconciliation mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** Timing differences (unpresented cheques, uncleared deposits) need only ADJUSTMENT in the BRS; ERRORS need correction, sometimes in the cash book itself — listing every difference as an "error", or adjusting timing differences into the cash book before the statement, misplaces the two families and loses the classification mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** Start by naming the BALANCE TYPE you have (cash book debit = favourable) and the TARGET balance; unpresented cheques are SUBTRACTED from the cash-book side, uncleared deposits ADDED — reversing these two directions is the single most common BRS error and the first thing the marking scheme checks.

**EXAM TRAP:** The AMENDED cash book absorbs items the firm knew only now — bank charges, direct deposits, dishonoured cheques — while purely timing items (unpresented cheques) wait for the BRS; putting timing differences into the amended cash book defeats the method and loses the adjustment-selection mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** When a BRS is prepared from the PASS BOOK balance, every adjustment direction REVERSES relative to the cash-book method — unpresented cheques are ADDED; relying on cash-book-side reflexes produces a statement that disagrees with both balances, the error the question is built to catch.

**EXAM TRAP:** Depreciation is a NON-CASH expense allocating COST — it is not a valuation of the asset's market price, and it applies to LAND never (inexhaustible); writing "depreciation saves money" instead of "spreads cost and matches expense to revenue" misses the matching principle behind the entry.

**EXAM TRAP:** The journal entry is Depreciation A/c Dr. to Asset/Provision A/c — depreciation never touches CASH; and charging it to the asset account directly versus a provision account changes the balance-sheet presentation, a distinction the question usually tests with the provision method.

**EXAM TRAP:** SLM charges a CONSTANT amount on original cost; WDV charges a CONSTANT RATE on the declining balance — so WDV depreciation falls each year and the asset never reduces to zero; quoting equal annual amounts under WDV, or applying the same rate logic to SLM, loses the method mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** Under the PROVISION method the asset account stays at COST and the provision account accumulates — the asset's book value is cost minus provision; writing accumulated depreciation inside the asset account and then also showing a provision is double-counting, the standard presentation error.

**EXAM TRAP:** On sale, profit or loss = sale proceeds − BOOK VALUE (cost − provision to date), not sale proceeds − original cost; and depreciation is charged UP TO THE DATE OF SALE — skipping the part-year depreciation first inflates the profit and loses both the adjustment and the profit marks.

**EXAM TRAP:** Three days of grace are added only when the bill is payable AFTER DATE or AFTER SIGHT — demand bills get none; and when the due date falls on an emergency/public holiday it moves to the PRECEDING business day — quoting due dates without grace days or the holiday rule loses the date mark every time.

**EXAM TRAP:** A promissory note has TWO parties (maker who PROMISES to pay, payee who receives) while a bill of exchange has THREE (drawer, drawee, payee) — the maker's unconditional promise is the note's essence; calling the drawee of a note a third party confuses the instruments and loses the comparison mark.

**EXAM TRAP:** A cheque is always drawn ON A BANK and payable on DEMAND — a three-month post-dated instrument is a bill, not a cheque; and crossing a cheque (general or special) directs it into an ACCOUNT, it does not stop transfer of ownership — mixing crossing with endorsement loses the negotiability mark.
